A_target.statement:
Let $p$ be prime and $m = \displaystyle \sum_i m_i p^i$, $n = \displaystyle \sum_i n_i p^i$ in base $p$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \binom m n \equiv \prod_i \binom {m_i} {n_i} \pmod p$

substitutions.the exponent p: the powers p^i in the base-p expansion of m

derived.the expanded product: a generating function whose coefficients are products of digit binomials

object_map.reformulation: Compute (1 + x)^m in GF(p)[x] digit by digit using the Frobenius identity, and compare coefficients.

validity_conditions: The base-p digits satisfy 0 <= m_i < p, so exponents of the expanded product are distinct.
C(m_i, n_i) = 0 when n_i > m_i, matching the vanishing of the coefficient.
proof_plan: By the source result and induction, $\paren {1 + x}^{p^i} = 1 + x^{p^i}$ in $\GF p \sqbrk x$.

Hence:
:$\displaystyle \paren {1 + x}^m = \prod_i \paren {1 + x}^{m_i p^i} = \prod_i \paren {1 + x^{p^i} }^{m_i} = \prod_i \sum_{k_i \mathop = 0}^{m_i} \binom {m_i} {k_i} x^{k_i p^i}$

As $0 \le k_i \le m_i < p$, each exponent $\sum_i k_i p^i$ arises from exactly one choice of digits.
So the coefficient of $x^n$ is $\displaystyle \prod_i \binom {m_i} {n_i}$.

Comparing with the coefficient $\dbinom m n$ of $x^n$ in $\paren {1 + x}^m$ gives [[Lucas' Theorem]].
{{qed}}
